S042.note: Belgium cannot vote on the vague protocol proposal since article 41 bis spells out the right of individual petition while the protocol's content is unknown; a voting point, but its substance is where the petition right goes.

S047.note: Lebanon backs the Nigerian draft Optional Protocol on individual petitions to secure the widest support for that right and proposes two drafting changes to it.

S048.note: India on the draft protocol on individual petitions: there should be real machinery for individuals' grievances, with detailed comments on its articles and preamble.

S053.note: Libya welcomes the adopted Covenants as a whole, explains its votes for both and for the Optional Protocol.

S057.note: Romania explains its vote for both Covenants as a whole, adding that they should be open to all States (borderline: the one specific point is the signature clause).

S058.note: Algeria's closing remarks associating itself with Tanzania and commending the work on the Covenants.

S066.note: Mrs Roosevelt: adopting the declaration is the session's great achievement and its adoption should not be deferred, against the Soviet postponement proposal.

S070.note: Ethiopia ranges over the draft covenant: the first eighteen articles, its breadth of wording, inclusion of ESC rights, implementation later, and a small amendment to article 3; none dominates.

S072.note: Belgium wants economic, social and cultural rights in the covenant but, given overlap with the specialized agencies, proposes referring the issue back to the Commission.

S081.note: Ukrainian SSR defends its vote for the Afghan-Saudi self-determination amendment and rebuts the UK on the Soviet republics' free association (with a complaint about the Chair).

S085.note: Argentina explains its abstention on a sub-paragraph referring to proposals for UN complaint machinery, stressing its support for the right of petition (some overlap with implementation).

S087.note: Venezuela's vote for the resolution does not prejudge its final attitude to the revised draft covenant as a whole.

S106.note: Afghanistan: self-determination must be in both covenants; weighs the US compromise wording and asks for roll-call votes on the self-determination amendments.

S109.note: Lebanon objects that the revised Syrian draft lets non-parties, NGOs, groups and individuals complain equally with States parties, unlike draft article 52, and wants the original text (overlaps implementation).

S115.note: Uruguay invokes Artigas and its own emancipation to uphold the principle of self-determination of peoples.

S120.note: Mrs Roosevelt on the universality of self-determination and the various amendments (US, Indian, five-Power plebiscite, Saudi) to the self-determination resolution.

S124.note: India revises its amendment to affirm self-determination of all peoples, including those of Non-Self-Governing and Trust Territories.

S162.note: New Zealand: self-determination is a political principle outside the Third Committee's remit, so it will vote against the Afghan draft resolution.

S166.note: USSR opposes the three-Power amendment on permanent sovereignty over natural resources and comments on the Indian amendment to the self-determination resolution.

S167.note: Israel explains its votes on the self-determination resolution and the three-Power and Indian amendments.

S202.note: Ireland calls self-determination the master-principle of the Charter and supports the joint draft resolution and the proposed commissions on it.

S228.note: Australia's general comments: the draft declaration as a whole is adequate and should keep its balance, and the covenant and implementation also deserve attention.

S242.note: Australia proposes wording for the report: human rights cannot be secured by enforcement alone, nationally or internationally, and the UN should educate peoples, i.e. on implementation.

S253.note: UK: a preamble would help, and the Declaration should be a brief statement of principles, unlike the legally drafted Convention.

S286.note: India: the Commission should decide in principle who is granted the right of petition before a drafting group works out details.

S307.note: Philippines on the draft covenant as a whole: imperfect (no asylum, no ESC rights, accession) but should be transmitted under the Lebanese resolution, not abandoned.

S309.note: Philippines disagrees with those dissatisfied with the Commission's work on the covenant (one sentence, overall assessment; low confidence).

S321.note: Mrs Roosevelt: the Uruguayan Attorney-General plan for petitions is too complicated; petitions from individuals and NGOs could go in a simpler separate protocol; articles 19-41 acceptable.

S327.note: UK against India's view that international measures of implementation need not be in the Covenant: without them the Covenant would be a mere declaration.

S338.note: Yugoslavia: the Covenant cannot grant individuals and NGOs the right of petition; international action only for threats to peace, petition only under domestic law.

S390.note: USSR on how the Commission should proceed, then a reservation that there should be a single covenant and ESC rights cannot be separated (mixed with procedure; the substantive part is one covenant or two).

S422.note: Uruguay is satisfied with the session's work; all principles of the two draft covenants are already in its constitution.

S426.note: USSR on the meanings of 'Bill', 'Charter', 'Convention', 'Covenant' and 'Treaty' in naming the instruments, within the declaration-versus-convention debate (terminological).

S432.note: Belgium on the system of periodic reports: it would put States parties at a disadvantage against non-parties and discourage accession.

S435.note: Consultative Council of Jewish Organizations: State-to-State complaints are inadequate; individuals need a right of complaint at the international level.

S442.note: India replies to the Belgian proposal on less-developed peoples that its constitution applies to every part of its territory, i.e. territorial application (uncertain: raised in the reservations debate).

S446.note: France on whether the Belgian proposal can be treated within the general discussion of reservations, and transmitting it with the other reservation proposals (partly procedural).

S449.note: Greece explains its vote for the joint self-determination proposals as a step towards implementing the right.

S452.note: China: take no vote yet and proceed on the assumption that the bill will be a General Assembly resolution, i.e. its legal form.

S453.note: Panama urges keeping the draft declaration's article on the right of petition, which was later dropped from the declaration.
